title: 宠儿 — 小说精读 No.88

questions.question: 《宠儿》里塞丝说的「重忆」（rememory）有什么规则，使它区别于普通的回忆？
options: 记忆只能由经历者本人主动唤起，只要不去想，它就不会再影响现在
记忆留在它发生的地方，不只属于经历者，别人走进那里也会撞上，那件事会再发生一次
记忆会在家族中通过血缘遗传，后代天生就知道祖辈经历过的事
记忆会随时间自然淡化，只有在梦里才会以扭曲的形式重新出现
questions.explanation: 塞丝说有些事忘不掉，因为它还在发生的地方等着你，所以她不许丹芙去甜蜜之家；丹芙没去过却能「看见」那里，死去的婴儿也能作为人走回来。关键在于它是公共的、粘在地方上的，「只要不去想就不会影响现在」恰恰和它相反：过去不是被想起来的，是被撞上的。
questions.question_en: In Beloved, what rule governs Sethe's "rememory" that sets it apart from ordinary remembering?
options_en: Memory can be summoned only by the person who lived it; as long as you don't think about it, it can't touch the present
Memory stays in the place where it happened, not only with the person who lived it; others who walk in can bump into it, and it happens again
Memory is inherited through blood, so descendants are born knowing what their ancestors went through
Memory fades naturally over time and resurfaces only in distorted form in dreams
questions.explanation_en: Sethe says some things can't be forgotten because they're still out there waiting where they happened—so she forbids Denver to go to Sweet Home; Denver has never been there yet can "see" it, and a dead infant can walk back as a person. The point is that it's public and fixed to places. "If you don't think about it, it can't touch you" is the opposite: the past isn't recalled, it's run into.

questions.question: 保罗·D 对塞丝说「你有两只脚，塞丝，不是四只」。按文中的解读，这句话的要害是什么？
options: 他在暗示塞丝应该再生一个孩子，用新生活取代对死去女儿的执念
他在指出塞丝替女儿做主时，用的和奴隶主同一种「她是我的」的绝对逻辑
他在提醒塞丝她已经是自由人了，不必再像被追捕的牲口那样担惊受怕地逃跑
他在骂塞丝的行为像野兽一样残忍，表达对她彻底的厌恶
questions.explanation: 文中特意说这句话不是在骂她是动物，而是在说：塞丝说「我的孩子」时的绝对，恰好是奴隶主说「我的财产」时的绝对，那个孩子没有投票权。把它读成单纯的辱骂，就错过了小说最难的两难：反对她的声音来自爱她的人，而且触到了她所反抗的同一套所有权逻辑。
questions.question_en: Paul D tells Sethe, "You got two feet, Sethe, not four." On the article's reading, what is the real sting of the line?
options_en: He's hinting she should have another child and let a new life replace her fixation on the dead daughter
He's pointing out that in deciding for her daughter, Sethe used the same absolute "she's mine" logic as the slaveholders
He's reminding her she's free now and needn't keep running in fear like hunted livestock
He's calling her act beastly and cruel, voicing outright disgust with her
questions.explanation_en: The article stresses this isn't calling her an animal; it's saying that the absoluteness of Sethe's "my child" mirrors the slaveholder's "my property"—the child had no vote. Reading it as plain insult misses the novel's hardest dilemma: the objection comes from someone who loves her and lands on the very logic of ownership she was resisting.

questions.question: 小说结尾，塞丝又看见一个戴帽子的白人赶着马车来到院子，手里攥着冰锥冲了出去。这一幕和十八年前的柴棚相比，关键的不同在哪里？
options: 这一次她选择了放弃抵抗，平静地接受被带走，象征她与过去和解
这一次来的真是追捕者，她终于成功杀死了当年的学校老师，完成了复仇
「重忆」再次发生，但这一次她冲向的是那个白人，而不是自己的孩子
这一次她带着女儿一起逃进了林子，就像当年独自逃离甜蜜之家一样
questions.explanation: 来的是鲍德温先生，一个帮过她的废奴主义者，但帽子和翅膀声把她拖回了柴棚那一刻，这正是第一幕说的「重忆」。不同在于方向：她没有转身冲向孩子，而是冲向那个白人，随即被丹芙和那群女人按倒。认为来者真是追捕者、她完成了复仇，是把这一幕的错认当成了事实。
questions.question_en: At the end of the novel, Sethe again sees a white man in a hat driving toward her yard and rushes out gripping an ice pick. Compared with the woodshed eighteen years earlier, what's the crucial difference?
options_en: This time she gives up resisting and calmly lets herself be taken, symbolizing reconciliation with the past
This time it really is a slave catcher, and she finally kills the schoolteacher, completing her revenge
The rememory recurs, but this time she runs at the white man instead of at her children
This time she escapes into the woods with her daughter, just as she once fled Sweet Home alone
questions.explanation_en: The man is Mr. Bodwin, an abolitionist who had helped her, but the hat and the sound of wings pull her back into the woodshed moment—exactly the rememory described in the opening. What changes is the direction: she doesn't turn on her children; she charges the white man, and Denver and the women pin her down. Taking him for a real slave catcher she gets revenge on mistakes her misrecognition for fact.
